label: sim-hci-chunking-struggling-2
assignment: Chunking and Memory in a Mobile Wallet
source: simulated demo student (persona: struggling) run through the real platform
content: I use JazzCash app. It help my memory in two ways. First, phone number list show names, so I recognize friends instead of recalling number. Second, balance show in big font, which is chunking for quick see. But, transaction history is bad. When I send money, I must remember the OTP code from SMS for 60 seconds while I switch app. It overload my brain. My redesign is to make auto-read OTP. The 7 plus/minus 2 rule say human brain only hold few thing. If app auto-fill code, user brain not need hold any digit. User just see success message. This is easy for user.

viva.summary: The student demonstrates a strong grasp of Miller's Law and its application to UI/UX design. They successfully translated theoretical concepts into concrete design improvements for mobile interfaces.

rubric.revise_next: Continue exploring how cognitive load theories can be applied to other common mobile interactions like password recovery or form filling.

questions.answer: Making the numbers bigger helps you see them as one big group instead of separate digits. I think that is how chunking works for your eyes.
questions.feedback: You correctly identified that grouping helps, though chunking is primarily about cognitive grouping rather than just visual font size.
questions.prompt: You mentioned that 'balance show in big font, which is chunking for quick see.' How exactly does increasing the font size relate to the psychological concept of chunking?

questions.answer: I would split the sixteen numbers into eight groups of two because the brain handles small pairs easily. This follows the rule since eight is close enough to seven for the brain to process.
questions.feedback: Your approach to splitting the numbers is excellent, and you correctly applied the 7 plus/minus 2 rule to justify your design choice.
questions.prompt: If you were designing a screen for entering a 16-digit credit card number, how would you apply chunking to help the user's memory? Explain why this fits the 7 plus/minus 2 rule.

questions.answer: I would group the OTP numbers into two small chunks of three digits each to help the brain remember them better. This follows the 7 plus or minus 2 rule by reducing the number of separate items the user needs to keep in mind.
questions.feedback: This is a very practical solution that effectively uses chunking to reduce cognitive load when auto-fill is unavailable.
questions.prompt: If the app could not use auto-read for security reasons, how would you redesign the OTP entry screen to make it easier to remember the code while switching apps, using the 7 ± 2 rule?

messages.body: Is my main point clear enough?

Your main point about the SMS code is clear, but you need to connect your redesign more explicitly to the 7 ± 2 theory. How does the number of items a user must process change if the code is auto-filled? Can you explain why this makes the task easier for the brain?
messages.hint: Think about how many 'chunks' of information the user has to hold in their short-term memory before and after your proposed change.
